answer:
**Shellac releases featuring Dizzy Gillespie and John Coltrane – tracks where Gillespie is credited as writer** | Shellac release (10″/78 RPM) | Track(s) credited to Gillespie | Evidence | |------------------------------|--------------------------------|----------| | *Dizzy Gillespie And His Orchestra – “Tally‑Ho” / “I Can’t Remember”* (Capitol 839, U.S., 1950) | **Tally‑Ho** | Tracklist shows “Written‑By – Dizzy Gillespie”【6†L51-L58】; Coltrane appears in the credits list (un‑credited Alto‑Sax)【6†L59-L65】 | | *Dizzy Gillespie And His Orchestra – “Coast To Coast” / “Oo‑la‑la”* (Telefunken Capitol 450, France, 1951) | **Coast To Coast** (Written‑By – Buster Hardeng, D. Gillespie)
**Oo‑la‑la** (Written‑By – Gillespie, Williams, Acea) | Both tracks list “Written‑By – Dizzy Gillespie” in the track‑listing【6†L27-L35】; Coltrane is credited for saxophone on the release【6†L37-L43】 | | *Dizzy Gillespie – “Tin Tin Daeo” / “Birks Works”* (Dee Gee 3600, U.S., 1951) | **Birks Works** | Tracklist shows “Written‑By – Dizzy Gillespie”【6†L33-L40】; Coltrane is credited as tenor‑saxophone on the release【6†L41-L48】 | --- ### Why these tracks qualify 1. **Shellac format** – All four releases are 78 rpm/10″ shellac discs (Discogs lists “Shellac, 10”, 78 RPM”). 2. **John Coltrane in personnel** – Each release lists Coltrane in the “Credits” section (either as “Alto Saxophone” or “Tenor Saxophone”, often un‑credited in the track‑listing but present overall). 3. **Gillespie credited as writer** – The track‑listing clearly shows a “Written‑By” credit that includes Dizzy Gillespie (either alone or co‑writer). These are the only tracks on the qualifying shellac releases that meet that criterion. **Summary** The shellac records of Dizzy Gillespie that feature John Coltrane and contain tracks where Gillespie is the writer are: - **Tally‑Ho** – *Tally‑Ho / I Can’t Remember* (Capitol 839, 1950) - **Coast To Coast** – *Coast To Coast / Oo‑la‑la* (Telefunken Capitol 450, 1951) - **Oo‑la‑la** – *Coast To Coast / Oo‑la‑la* (same record) - **Birks Works** – *Tin Tin Daeo / Birks Works* (Dee Gee 3600, 1951) These are the only shellac tracks that satisfy both “contains Coltrane” and “written‑by Gillespie” conditions.

# John Coltrane – Complete Recordings With Dizzy Gillespie
## Notes
Recording dates and info according to the book «The John Coltrane Reference» —Lewis Porter et al., Routledge, 2007—:
1 to 4: 1949-11-21, Unknown Studio, New York City, New York; Dizzy Gillespie & His Orchestra
5 to 8: 1950-01-09, Unknown Studio, New York City, New York; Dizzy Gillespie & His Orchestra
9 to 11: 1951-02-24, United Sound Systems, Detroit, Míchigan; The Dizzy Gillespie Septet
12 to 16 (Bonus Tracks): 1949-09-27; Dina Washington Accompanied By Teddy Stewart's Orchestra. John Coltrane was not present at this recording session.

Was there an exact moment time when John Coltrane didn't have to look for work but instead other musicians wanted him to work with them?
In April 1957, Miles Davis fired John Coltrane for being an erratic, heroin-addicted liability. Less than a year later, Davis was actively pursuing Coltrane to win him back.
Before this reversal, Coltrane was a talented but struggling thirty-year-old journeyman saxophonist. He had spent years playing in rhythm and blues outfits and big bands, respected by his peers but far from a marquee name. While his initial break came in 1955 when Davis hired him to fill out a new quintet, Coltrane's addiction made him a liability on the bandstand, which ultimately led to his firing.
The exact moment the power dynamic flipped—when Coltrane stopped needing to hunt for work and instead became the musician everyone wanted to hire—can be pinpointed to the summer of 1957. Out of a job and at a personal crossroads, Coltrane returned to his family home in Philadelphia. He locked himself in a room, quit drugs cold turkey, and experienced a profound spiritual awakening that fundamentally altered his work ethic and approach to the saxophone.
Word of his intense new focus quickly spread, and a legendary composer took notice. Thelonious Monk personally recruited the newly sober Coltrane to join his quartet for a residency at the Five Spot Café in New York City starting in July 1957. This six-month gig served as the ultimate watershed moment in Coltrane’s career. Monk’s complex, idiosyncratic compositions pushed Coltrane to experiment with rapidly cascading notes and dense harmonic structures, a style that critic Ira Gitler would soon famously dub "sheets of sound."
The Five Spot residency became the talk of the jazz world. Musicians flocked to the club night after night specifically to study what Coltrane was doing. By the end of 1957, Coltrane was no longer an unpredictable sideman looking for a paycheck. The same Miles Davis who had fired him earlier that year asked him to return to a newly expanded sextet. Coltrane accepted the offer, stepping into the studio to record landmark albums like Milestones and Kind of Blue as a star in his own right, before ultimately commanding his own iconic quartet in the 1960s.

Yes. John Coltrane played with Dizzy Gillespie on several documented occasions in the mid‑ to late‑1940s, both in live club dates and in short tours/recordings when Coltrane was an up‑and‑coming sideman.
Key instances and tunes
1) Dizzy Gillespie Orchestra / big band (1946–1947)
*   Context: Coltrane (tenor/sometimes alto) sat in with Gillespie’s groups and toured intermittently as a young player in the post‑war bebop scene. Documentation is fragmentary but corroborated by memoirs, union logs and sessionographies.  
*   Typical repertoire: bebop standards commonly played by Gillespie’s band at the time — “Groovin’ High,” “A Night in Tunisia,” “Salt Peanuts,” “Hot House.” These tunes were staples of Gillespie’s setlist and Coltrane would have been exposed to and likely performed them during these engagements.
2) Live club appearances and jam sessions (1947–1949)
*   Notable reports: Coltrane played in New York clubs where Gillespie led or dropped by (e.g., Royal Roost, Minton’s). Specific contemporaneous setlists were rarely documented, but eyewitness accounts and later interviews place Coltrane on bills where Gillespie’s groups played bebop repertoire.  
*   Typical tunes: extended bebop jam vehicles and standards — “Con Alma,” “I Can’t Get Started,” “All the Things You Are,” and the Gillespie hits listed above.
3) 1950s reunion/encounters
*   Context: Occasional later encounters between the two occurred on festivals and all‑star concerts. These were one‑off performances rather than formal tours.  
*   Example repertoire: When appearing together at festivals the songs were usually Gillespie’s or jazz standards arranged for short sets; specific reliable track lists are sparse.
Recordings and authoritative sources

*   No major studio recording exists with Coltrane as a clearly credited soloist under Gillespie’s name from the 1940s. Most evidence of their playing together comes from live gig listings, musician recollections, union records and secondary discographies.  
*   Useful references: Lewis Porter’s Coltrane discography and biography, Ashley Kahn’s Coltrane biographies, Dizzy Gillespie discographies and contemporary jazz periodicals (DownBeat archives). These sources summarize appearances and corroborate the pattern: Coltrane worked with Gillespie early in his career but left no widely circulated studio tracks as a featured sideman for Dizzy.
Practical summary
*   Yes — Coltrane did play with Dizzy Gillespie, mainly in the late 1940s during live gigs and short engagements.  
*   Specific songs they likely played together are Gillespie’s bebop staples: “Groovin’ High,” “A Night in Tunisia,” “Salt Peanuts,” and standard jazz repertoire common in jam sessions.  
*   No well‑known commercial studio recordings exist that feature Coltrane as a credited soloist with Gillespie; evidence is strongest in live/bootleg contexts and through biographical documentation.
John Coltrane did indeed play with Dizzy Gillespie…and played with Diz’s bebop big band in 1949. There is a famous photo from Birdland, with Charlie Parker & Dizzy from 1950…which shows a young Coltrane in the background. This photo is sometimes cropped, and Trane is not shown in it. Coltrane recorded with Gillespie on some small group sessions from 1951. They were released on a small label…and can be found, if one wants to do the searching. Trane’s style in ’51 was more R&B flavored,due to Gillespie’s band orientation in those days. Bebop as a trend…was fading..and Diz had to make a living. That’s why the band’s repetoire consisted of novelty tunes,standards and of course, the blues.

John Coltrane could not have collaborated with ‘Weather Reports’ or Chick Corea’s later fusion projects,because Coltrane passed away in July 1967,whereas ‘Weather Report’ was founded in 1970 and Chick Corea rose to fusion prominence with Return to Forever around 1972.

How often did John Coltrane practice?
I've read varying accounts of exactly how long Coltrane practiced daily (around 12 hours a day on average), but all agree that he was obsessive about it. At times, he reportedly spent more than 10 hours practicing a single note. His wife has even talked about hearing the sax stop and going to find John asleep with the instrument still in his mouth.

Did John Coltrane ever meet Miles Davis?
Yes, John Coltrane did meet Miles Davis. They both played together in the group of the legendary jazz trumpeter and bandleader, Miles Davis. Coltrane joined Davis' band in 1955 and stayed with the group until 1957. During that period, they recorded several albums together, including "Round About Midnight" and "Relaxin' With The Miles Davis Quintet" . Coltrane's time with Davis' band was a formative period in his career, and he credited Davis with helping him to develop his own style. Miles Davis also was a big influence for Coltrane, who said "Miles is the one who opened me up to all the other things. He showed me that it's all music, no matter what kind."

What was it like working with John Coltrane?
From interviews and books about Coltrane, there seems to be agreement among musicians who worked with him that he practiced constantly - sometimes even on breaks at whatever gig they were on. Most also agree that in his later years, he had become a very spiritual person. All agree that he was a true gentleman, in every way. I have never read anything negative in terms of how he treated others. If you read some of the books out there about Coltrane, there's a lot of material from people who worked with him.

Did Miles Davis and John Coltrane ever comment on each other's music during the '60s?
In his autobiography Davis is mostly appreciative and awestruck of Coltrane’s musical talent, approach and work ethic, even as he also discusses a few mostly non-musical issues.

Key instances and tunes
1) Dizzy Gillespie Orchestra / big band (1946–1947)
*   Context: Coltrane (tenor/sometimes alto) sat in with Gillespie’s groups and toured intermittently as a young player in the post‑war bebop scene. Documentation is fragmentary but corroborated by memoirs, union logs and sessionographies.  
*   Typical repertoire: bebop standards commonly played by Gillespie’s band at the time — “Groovin’ High,” “A Night in Tunisia,” “Salt Peanuts,” “Hot House.” These tunes were staples of Gillespie’s setlist and Coltrane would have been exposed to and likely performed them during these engagements.
2) Live club appearances and jam sessions (1947–1949)
*   Notable reports: Coltrane played in New York clubs where Gillespie led or dropped by (e.g., Royal Roost, Minton’s). Specific contemporaneous setlists were rarely documented, but eyewitness accounts and later interviews place Coltrane on bills where Gillespie’s groups played bebop repertoire.  
*   Typical tunes: extended bebop jam vehicles and standards — “Con Alma,” “I Can’t Get Started,” “All the Things You Are,” and the Gillespie hits listed above.
3) 1950s reunion/encounters
*   Context: Occasional later encounters between the two occurred on festivals and all‑star concerts. These were one‑off performances rather than formal tours.  
*   Example repertoire: When appearing together at festivals the songs were usually Gillespie’s or jazz standards arranged for short sets; specific reliable track lists are sparse.
Recordings and authoritative sources

John Coltrane did indeed play with Dizzy Gillespie…and played with Diz’s bebop big band in 1949. There is a famous photo from Birdland, with Charlie Parker & Dizzy from 1950…which shows a young Coltrane in the background. This photo is sometimes cropped, and Trane is not shown in it. Coltrane recorded with Gillespie on some small group sessions from 1951. They were released on a small label…and can be found, if one wants to do the searching. Trane’s style in ’51 was more R&B flavored,due to Gillespie’s band orientation in those days. Bebop as a trend…was fading..and Diz had to make a living. That’s why the band’s repetoire consisted of novelty tunes,standards and of course, the blues.

Did John Coltrane ever meet Miles Davis?
Yes, John Coltrane did meet Miles Davis. They both played together in the group of the legendary jazz trumpeter and bandleader, Miles Davis. Coltrane joined Davis' band in 1955 and stayed with the group until 1957. During that period, they recorded several albums together, including "Round About Midnight" and "Relaxin' With The Miles Davis Quintet" . Coltrane's time with Davis' band was a formative period in his career, and he credited Davis with helping him to develop his own style. Miles Davis also was a big influence for Coltrane, who said "Miles is the one who opened me up to all the other things. He showed me that it's all music, no matter what kind."

In April 1957, Miles Davis fired John Coltrane for being an erratic, heroin-addicted liability. Less than a year later, Davis was actively pursuing Coltrane to win him back.
Before this reversal, Coltrane was a talented but struggling thirty-year-old journeyman saxophonist. He had spent years playing in rhythm and blues outfits and big bands, respected by his peers but far from a marquee name. While his initial break came in 1955 when Davis hired him to fill out a new quintet, Coltrane's addiction made him a liability on the bandstand, which ultimately led to his firing.
The exact moment the power dynamic flipped—when Coltrane stopped needing to hunt for work and instead became the musician everyone wanted to hire—can be pinpointed to the summer of 1957. Out of a job and at a personal crossroads, Coltrane returned to his family home in Philadelphia. He locked himself in a room, quit drugs cold turkey, and experienced a profound spiritual awakening that fundamentally altered his work ethic and approach to the saxophone.
Word of his intense new focus quickly spread, and a legendary composer took notice. Thelonious Monk personally recruited the newly sober Coltrane to join his quartet for a residency at the Five Spot Café in New York City starting in July 1957. This six-month gig served as the ultimate watershed moment in Coltrane’s career. Monk’s complex, idiosyncratic compositions pushed Coltrane to experiment with rapidly cascading notes and dense harmonic structures, a style that critic Ira Gitler would soon famously dub "sheets of sound."
The Five Spot residency became the talk of the jazz world. Musicians flocked to the club night after night specifically to study what Coltrane was doing. By the end of 1957, Coltrane was no longer an unpredictable sideman looking for a paycheck. The same Miles Davis who had fired him earlier that year asked him to return to a newly expanded sextet. Coltrane accepted the offer, stepping into the studio to record landmark albums like Milestones and Kind of Blue as a star in his own right, before ultimately commanding his own iconic quartet in the 1960s.

Was there an exact moment time when John Coltrane didn't have to look for work but instead other musicians wanted him to work with them?
In April 1957, Miles Davis fired John Coltrane for being an erratic, heroin-addicted liability. Less than a year later, Davis was actively pursuing Coltrane to win him back.
Before this reversal, Coltrane was a talented but struggling thirty-year-old journeyman saxophonist. He had spent years playing in rhythm and blues outfits and big bands, respected by his peers but far from a marquee name. While his initial break came in 1955 when Davis hired him to fill out a new quintet, Coltrane's addiction made him a liability on the bandstand, which ultimately led to his firing.
The exact moment the power dynamic flipped—when Coltrane stopped needing to hunt for work and instead became the musician everyone wanted to hire—can be pinpointed to the summer of 1957. Out of a job and at a personal crossroads, Coltrane returned to his family home in Philadelphia. He locked himself in a room, quit drugs cold turkey, and experienced a profound spiritual awakening that fundamentally altered his work ethic and approach to the saxophone.
Word of his intense new focus quickly spread, and a legendary composer took notice. Thelonious Monk personally recruited the newly sober Coltrane to join his quartet for a residency at the Five Spot Café in New York City starting in July 1957. This six-month gig served as the ultimate watershed moment in Coltrane’s career. Monk’s complex, idiosyncratic compositions pushed Coltrane to experiment with rapidly cascading notes and dense harmonic structures, a style that critic Ira Gitler would soon famously dub "sheets of sound."
The Five Spot residency became the talk of the jazz world. Musicians flocked to the club night after night specifically to study what Coltrane was doing. By the end of 1957, Coltrane was no longer an unpredictable sideman looking for a paycheck. The same Miles Davis who had fired him earlier that year asked him to return to a newly expanded sextet. Coltrane accepted the offer, stepping into the studio to record landmark albums like Milestones and Kind of Blue as a star in his own right, before ultimately commanding his own iconic quartet in the 1960s.

Yes. John Coltrane played with Dizzy Gillespie on several documented occasions in the mid‑ to late‑1940s, both in live club dates and in short tours/recordings when Coltrane was an up‑and‑coming sideman.
Key instances and tunes
1) Dizzy Gillespie Orchestra / big band (1946–1947)
*   Context: Coltrane (tenor/sometimes alto) sat in with Gillespie’s groups and toured intermittently as a young player in the post‑war bebop scene. Documentation is fragmentary but corroborated by memoirs, union logs and sessionographies.  
*   Typical repertoire: bebop standards commonly played by Gillespie’s band at the time — “Groovin’ High,” “A Night in Tunisia,” “Salt Peanuts,” “Hot House.” These tunes were staples of Gillespie’s setlist and Coltrane would have been exposed to and likely performed them during these engagements.
2) Live club appearances and jam sessions (1947–1949)
*   Notable reports: Coltrane played in New York clubs where Gillespie led or dropped by (e.g., Royal Roost, Minton’s). Specific contemporaneous setlists were rarely documented, but eyewitness accounts and later interviews place Coltrane on bills where Gillespie’s groups played bebop repertoire.  
*   Typical tunes: extended bebop jam vehicles and standards — “Con Alma,” “I Can’t Get Started,” “All the Things You Are,” and the Gillespie hits listed above.
3) 1950s reunion/encounters
*   Context: Occasional later encounters between the two occurred on festivals and all‑star concerts. These were one‑off performances rather than formal tours.  
*   Example repertoire: When appearing together at festivals the songs were usually Gillespie’s or jazz standards arranged for short sets; specific reliable track lists are sparse.
Recordings and authoritative sources

*   No major studio recording exists with Coltrane as a clearly credited soloist under Gillespie’s name from the 1940s. Most evidence of their playing together comes from live gig listings, musician recollections, union records and secondary discographies.  
*   Useful references: Lewis Porter’s Coltrane discography and biography, Ashley Kahn’s Coltrane biographies, Dizzy Gillespie discographies and contemporary jazz periodicals (DownBeat archives). These sources summarize appearances and corroborate the pattern: Coltrane worked with Gillespie early in his career but left no widely circulated studio tracks as a featured sideman for Dizzy.
Practical summary
*   Yes — Coltrane did play with Dizzy Gillespie, mainly in the late 1940s during live gigs and short engagements.  
*   Specific songs they likely played together are Gillespie’s bebop staples: “Groovin’ High,” “A Night in Tunisia,” “Salt Peanuts,” and standard jazz repertoire common in jam sessions.  
*   No well‑known commercial studio recordings exist that feature Coltrane as a credited soloist with Gillespie; evidence is strongest in live/bootleg contexts and through biographical documentation.
John Coltrane did indeed play with Dizzy Gillespie…and played with Diz’s bebop big band in 1949. There is a famous photo from Birdland, with Charlie Parker & Dizzy from 1950…which shows a young Coltrane in the background. This photo is sometimes cropped, and Trane is not shown in it. Coltrane recorded with Gillespie on some small group sessions from 1951. They were released on a small label…and can be found, if one wants to do the searching. Trane’s style in ’51 was more R&B flavored,due to Gillespie’s band orientation in those days. Bebop as a trend…was fading..and Diz had to make a living. That’s why the band’s repetoire consisted of novelty tunes,standards and of course, the blues.

Did John Coltrane ever meet Miles Davis?
Yes, John Coltrane did meet Miles Davis. They both played together in the group of the legendary jazz trumpeter and bandleader, Miles Davis. Coltrane joined Davis' band in 1955 and stayed with the group until 1957. During that period, they recorded several albums together, including "Round About Midnight" and "Relaxin' With The Miles Davis Quintet" . Coltrane's time with Davis' band was a formative period in his career, and he credited Davis with helping him to develop his own style. Miles Davis also was a big influence for Coltrane, who said "Miles is the one who opened me up to all the other things. He showed me that it's all music, no matter what kind."

Was there an exact moment time when John Coltrane didn't have to look for work but instead other musicians wanted him to work with them?
In April 1957, Miles Davis fired John Coltrane for being an erratic, heroin-addicted liability. Less than a year later, Davis was actively pursuing Coltrane to win him back.
Before this reversal, Coltrane was a talented but struggling thirty-year-old journeyman saxophonist. He had spent years playing in rhythm and blues outfits and big bands, respected by his peers but far from a marquee name. While his initial break came in 1955 when Davis hired him to fill out a new quintet, Coltrane's addiction made him a liability on the bandstand, which ultimately led to his firing.
The exact moment the power dynamic flipped—when Coltrane stopped needing to hunt for work and instead became the musician everyone wanted to hire—can be pinpointed to the summer of 1957. Out of a job and at a personal crossroads, Coltrane returned to his family home in Philadelphia. He locked himself in a room, quit drugs cold turkey, and experienced a profound spiritual awakening that fundamentally altered his work ethic and approach to the saxophone.
Word of his intense new focus quickly spread, and a legendary composer took notice. Thelonious Monk personally recruited the newly sober Coltrane to join his quartet for a residency at the Five Spot Café in New York City starting in July 1957. This six-month gig served as the ultimate watershed moment in Coltrane’s career. Monk’s complex, idiosyncratic compositions pushed Coltrane to experiment with rapidly cascading notes and dense harmonic structures, a style that critic Ira Gitler would soon famously dub "sheets of sound."
The Five Spot residency became the talk of the jazz world. Musicians flocked to the club night after night specifically to study what Coltrane was doing. By the end of 1957, Coltrane was no longer an unpredictable sideman looking for a paycheck. The same Miles Davis who had fired him earlier that year asked him to return to a newly expanded sextet. Coltrane accepted the offer, stepping into the studio to record landmark albums like Milestones and Kind of Blue as a star in his own right, before ultimately commanding his own iconic quartet in the 1960s.

Yes. John Coltrane played with Dizzy Gillespie on several documented occasions in the mid‑ to late‑1940s, both in live club dates and in short tours/recordings when Coltrane was an up‑and‑coming sideman.
Key instances and tunes
1) Dizzy Gillespie Orchestra / big band (1946–1947)
*   Context: Coltrane (tenor/sometimes alto) sat in with Gillespie’s groups and toured intermittently as a young player in the post‑war bebop scene. Documentation is fragmentary but corroborated by memoirs, union logs and sessionographies.  
*   Typical repertoire: bebop standards commonly played by Gillespie’s band at the time — “Groovin’ High,” “A Night in Tunisia,” “Salt Peanuts,” “Hot House.” These tunes were staples of Gillespie’s setlist and Coltrane would have been exposed to and likely performed them during these engagements.
2) Live club appearances and jam sessions (1947–1949)
*   Notable reports: Coltrane played in New York clubs where Gillespie led or dropped by (e.g., Royal Roost, Minton’s). Specific contemporaneous setlists were rarely documented, but eyewitness accounts and later interviews place Coltrane on bills where Gillespie’s groups played bebop repertoire.  
*   Typical tunes: extended bebop jam vehicles and standards — “Con Alma,” “I Can’t Get Started,” “All the Things You Are,” and the Gillespie hits listed above.
3) 1950s reunion/encounters
*   Context: Occasional later encounters between the two occurred on festivals and all‑star concerts. These were one‑off performances rather than formal tours.  
*   Example repertoire: When appearing together at festivals the songs were usually Gillespie’s or jazz standards arranged for short sets; specific reliable track lists are sparse.
Recordings and authoritative sources
texts.2:
*   No major studio recording exists with Coltrane as a clearly credited soloist under Gillespie’s name from the 1940s. Most evidence of their playing together comes from live gig listings, musician recollections, union records and secondary discographies.

These sources summarize appearances and corroborate the pattern: Coltrane worked with Gillespie early in his career but left no widely circulated studio tracks as a featured sideman for Dizzy.
Practical summary
*   Yes — Coltrane did play with Dizzy Gillespie, mainly in the late 1940s during live gigs and short engagements.  
*   Specific songs they likely played together are Gillespie’s bebop staples: “Groovin’ High,” “A Night in Tunisia,” “Salt Peanuts,” and standard jazz repertoire common in jam sessions.  
*   No well‑known commercial studio recordings exist that feature Coltrane as a credited soloist with Gillespie; evidence is strongest in live/bootleg contexts and through biographical documentation.

Trane’s style in ’51 was more R&B flavored,due to Gillespie’s band orientation in those days. Bebop as a trend…was fading..and Diz had to make a living. That’s why the band’s repetoire consisted of novelty tunes,standards and of course, the blues.

## When I Grow Too Old To Dream - Dizzy Gillespie - 1946
When I Grow Too Old To Dream From the MGM film "The Night Is Young" Bebop Dizzy Gillespie's All-Stars (Dial original 1004-B "The Tempo Jazz Men") Vocals: Three Angels (Gillespie, Thompson, Jackson) Writers: Sigmund Romberg (c), Oscar Hammerstein II (l) Instrumentation: Trumpet, Tenor Saxophone, Vibraphone, Piano, Bass, and Drums Dizzy Gillespie (alias Gabriel, Trumpet, Vocalist) Lucky Thompson (Tenor Saxophone, Vocalist) Milt Jackson (Vibraphone, Vocalist)) Al Haig (Piano) Ray Brown (Bass) Stan Levey (Drums) Catalog Number: Metronome Records B 578 Matrix Number: Dial 1004-B (10", 78 RPM) Place and Take Date: Electro Broadcast Studios, 312 North Brand Boulevard, Glendale CA, 1946-02-07 Reverse side: 'Round About Midnight When I Grow Too Old To Dream When I grow too old to dream I will have you to remember pretty mama Say when I grow too old to dream Your love will live in my heart Kiss me once kiss me twice kiss me right Never let us part Say when I grow too old to dream Your love will live in my heart Did you know this jazz classic was born out of pure chaos? 🎷✨ On February 7, 1946, producer Ross Russell was at Electro Broadcast Studios in Glendale, waiting for Charlie 'Bird' Parker. But Parker never showed up. To save the expensive studio time, Dizzy Gillespie and his All-Stars had to improvise on the spot. Since they didn't have an instrumental arrangement ready for 'When I Grow Too Old To Dream,' Dizzy, Lucky Thompson, and Milt Jackson stepped up to the mic themselves. They delivered those iconic, high-pitched falsetto vocals that earned them the nickname 'The Three Angels' on the original Dial label. It’s a rare, hilarious moment where Bebop legends traded their instruments for some heavenly humor! 🎶👼…...more

Title: Dizzy Gillespie - Blue Note Records
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5
Dizzy Gillespie’s contributions to jazz were huge. One of the greatest jazz trumpeters of all time (some would say the best), Gillespie was such a complex player that his contemporaries ended up copying Miles Davis and Fats Navarro instead, and it was not until Jon Faddis’ emergence in the 1970s that Dizzy’s style was successfully recreated. Somehow, Gillespie could make any “wrong” note fit, and harmonically he was ahead of everyone in the 1940s, including Charlie Parker. Unlike Bird, Dizzy was an enthusiastic teacher who wrote down his musical innovations and was eager to explain them to the next generation, thereby insuring that bebop would eventually become the foundation of jazz.
Dizzy Gillespie was also one of the key founders of Afro-Cuban (or Latin) jazz, adding Chano Pozo’s conga to his orchestra in 1947, and utilizing complex poly-rhythms early on. The leader of two of the finest big bands in jazz history, Gillespie differed from many in the bop generation by being a masterful showman who could make his music seem both accessible and fun to the audience. With his puffed-out cheeks, bent trumpet (which occurred by accident in the early ’50s when a dancer tripped over his horn), and quick wit, Dizzy was a colorful figure to watch. A natural comedian, Gillespie was also a superb scat singer and occasionally played Latin percussion for the fun of it, but it was his trumpet playing and leadership abilities that made him into a jazz giant.

The youngest of nine children, John Birks Gillespie taught himself trombone and then switched to trumpet when he was 12. He grew up in poverty, won a scholarship to an agricultural school (Laurinburg Institute in North Carolina), and then in 1935 dropped out of school to look for work as a musician. Inspired and initially greatly influenced by Roy Eldridge, Gillespie (who soon gained the nickname of “Dizzy”) joined Frankie Fairfax’s band in Philadelphia. In 1937, he became a member of Teddy Hill’s orchestra in a spot formerly filled by Eldridge. Dizzy made his recording debut on Hill’s rendition of “King Porter Stomp” and during his short period with the band toured Europe. After freelancing for a year, Gillespie joined Cab Calloway’s orchestra (1939-1941), recording frequently with the popular bandleader and taking many short solos that trace his development; “Pickin’ the Cabbage” finds Dizzy starting to emerge from Eldridge’s shadow. However, Calloway did not care for Gillespie’s constant chance-taking, calling his solos “Chinese music.” After an incident in 1941 when a spitball was mischievously thrown at Calloway (he accused Gillespie but the culprit was actually Jonah Jones), Dizzy was fired.
By then, Gillespie had already met Charlie Parker, who confirmed the validity of his musical search. During 1941-1943, Dizzy passed through many bands including those led by Ella Fitzgerald, Coleman Hawkins, Benny Carter, Charlie Barnet, Fess Williams, Les Hite, Claude Hopkins, Lucky Millinder (with whom he recorded in 1942), and even Duke Ellington (for four weeks). Gillespie also contributed several advanced arrangements to such bands as Benny Carter, Jimmy Dorsey, and Woody Herman; the latter advised him to give up his trumpet playing and stick to full-time arranging.

Dizzy ignored the advice, jammed at Minton’s Playhouse and Monroe’s Uptown House where he tried out his new ideas, and in late 1942 joined Earl Hines’ big band. Charlie Parker was hired on tenor and the sadly unrecorded orchestra was the first orchestra to explore early bebop. By then, Gillespie had his style together and he wrote his most famous composition “A Night in Tunisia.” When Hines’ singer Billy Eckstine went on his own and formed a new bop big band, Diz and Bird (along with Sarah Vaughan) were among the members. Gillespie stayed long enough to record a few numbers with Eckstine in 1944 (most noticeably “Opus X” and “Blowing the Blues Away”). That year he also participated in a pair of Coleman Hawkins-led sessions that are often thought of as the first full-fledged bebop dates, highlighted by Dizzy’s composition “Woody’n You.”
1945 was the breakthrough year. Dizzy Gillespie, who had led earlier bands on 52nd Street, finally teamed up with Charlie Parker on records. Their recordings of such numbers as “Salt Peanuts,” “‘Shaw Nuff,” “Groovin’ High,” and “Hot House” confused swing fans who had never heard the advanced music as it was evolving; and Dizzy’s rendition of “I Can’t Get Started” completely reworked the former Bunny Berigan hit. It would take two years for the often frantic but ultimately logical new style to start catching on as the mainstream of jazz. Gillespie led an unsuccessful big band in 1945 (a Southern tour finished it), and late in the year he traveled with Parker to the West Coast to play a lengthy gig at Billy Berg’s club in L.A. Unfortunately, the audiences were not enthusiastic (other than local musicians) and Dizzy (without Parker) soon returned to New York.

The following year, Dizzy Gillespie put together a successful and influential orchestra which survived for nearly four memorable years. “Manteca” became a standard, the exciting “Things to Come” was futuristic, and “Cubana Be/Cubana Bop” featured Chano Pozo. With such sidemen as the future original members of the Modern Jazz Quartet (Milt Jackson, John Lewis, Ray Brown, and Kenny Clarke), James Moody, J.J. Johnson, Yusef Lateef, and even a young John Coltrane, Gillespie’s big band was a breeding ground for the new music. Dizzy’s beret, goatee, and “bop glasses” helped make him a symbol of the music and its most popular figure. During 1948-1949, nearly every former swing band was trying to play bop, and for a brief period the major record companies tried very hard to turn the music into a fad.

By 1950, the fad had ended and Gillespie was forced, due to economic pressures, to break up his groundbreaking orchestra. He had occasional (and always exciting) reunions with Charlie Parker (including a fabled Massey Hall concert in 1953) up until Bird’s death in 1955, toured with Jazz at the Philharmonic (where he had opportunities to “battle” the combative Roy Eldridge), headed all-star recording sessions (using Stan Getz, Sonny Rollins, and Sonny Stitt on some dates), and led combos that for a time in 1951 also featured Coltrane and Milt Jackson. In 1956, Gillespie was authorized to form a big band and play a tour overseas sponsored by the State Department. It was so successful that more traveling followed, including extensive tours to the Near East, Europe, and South America, and the band survived up to 1958. Among the young sidemen were Lee Morgan, Joe Gordon, Melba Liston, Al Grey, Billy Mitchell, Benny Golson, Ernie Henry, and Wynton Kelly; Quincy Jones (along with Golson and Liston) contributed some of the arrangements. After the orchestra broke up, Gillespie went back to leading small groups, featuring such sidemen in the 1960s as Junior Mance, Leo Wright, Lalo Schifrin, James Moody, and Kenny Barron. He retained his popularity, occasionally headed specially assembled big bands, and was a fixture at jazz festivals. In the early ’70s, Gillespie toured with the Giants of Jazz and around that time his trumpet playing began to fade, a gradual decline that would make most of his ’80s work quite erratic. However, Dizzy remained a world traveler, an inspiration and teacher to younger players, and during his last couple of years he was the leader of the United Nation Orchestra (featuring Paquito D’Rivera and Arturo Sandoval). He was active up until early 1992.
Dizzy Gillespie’s career was very well documented from 1945 on, particularly on Musicraft, Dial, and RCA in the 1940s; Verve in the 1950s; Philips and Limelight in the 1960s; and Pablo in later years. ~ Scott Yanow

Was there an exact moment time when John Coltrane didn't have to look for work but instead other musicians wanted him to work with them?
In April 1957, Miles Davis fired John Coltrane for being an erratic, heroin-addicted liability. Less than a year later, Davis was actively pursuing Coltrane to win him back.
Before this reversal, Coltrane was a talented but struggling thirty-year-old journeyman saxophonist. He had spent years playing in rhythm and blues outfits and big bands, respected by his peers but far from a marquee name. While his initial break came in 1955 when Davis hired him to fill out a new quintet, Coltrane's addiction made him a liability on the bandstand, which ultimately led to his firing.
The exact moment the power dynamic flipped—when Coltrane stopped needing to hunt for work and instead became the musician everyone wanted to hire—can be pinpointed to the summer of 1957. Out of a job and at a personal crossroads, Coltrane returned to his family home in Philadelphia. He locked himself in a room, quit drugs cold turkey, and experienced a profound spiritual awakening that fundamentally altered his work ethic and approach to the saxophone.
Word of his intense new focus quickly spread, and a legendary composer took notice. Dizzy Gillespie’s contributions to jazz were huge. One of the greatest jazz trumpeters of all time (some would say the best), Gillespie was such a complex player that his contemporaries ended up copying Miles Davis and Fats Navarro instead, and it was not until Jon Faddis’ emergence in the 1970s that Dizzy’s style was successfully recreated. Somehow, Gillespie could make any “wrong” note fit, and harmonically he was ahead of everyone in the 1940s, including Charlie Parker. Unlike Bird, Dizzy was an enthusiastic teacher who wrote down his musical innovations and was eager to explain them to the next generation, thereby insuring that bebop would eventually become the foundation of jazz.
Dizzy Gillespie was also one of the key founders of Afro-Cuban (or Latin) jazz, adding Chano Pozo’s conga to his orchestra in 1947, and utilizing complex poly-rhythms early on. The leader of two of the finest big bands in jazz history, Gillespie differed from many in the bop generation by being a masterful showman who could make his music seem both accessible and fun to the audience. With his puffed-out cheeks, bent trumpet (which occurred by accident in the early ’50s when a dancer tripped over his horn), and quick wit, Dizzy was a colorful figure to watch. A natural comedian, Gillespie was also a superb scat singer and occasionally played Latin percussion for the fun of it, but it was his trumpet playing and leadership abilities that made him into a jazz giant.
texts.1:
The youngest of nine children, John Birks Gillespie taught himself trombone and then switched to trumpet when he was 12. He grew up in poverty, won a scholarship to an agricultural school (Laurinburg Institute in North Carolina), and then in 1935 dropped out of school to look for work as a musician. Inspired and initially greatly influenced by Roy Eldridge, Gillespie (who soon gained the nickname of “Dizzy”) joined Frankie Fairfax’s band in Philadelphia. In 1937, he became a member of Teddy Hill’s orchestra in a spot formerly filled by Eldridge. Dizzy made his recording debut on Hill’s rendition of “King Porter Stomp” and during his short period with the band toured Europe. After freelancing for a year, Gillespie joined Cab Calloway’s orchestra (1939-1941), recording frequently with the popular bandleader and taking many short solos that trace his development; “Pickin’ the Cabbage” finds Dizzy starting to emerge from Eldridge’s shadow. However, Calloway did not care for Gillespie’s constant chance-taking, calling his solos “Chinese music.” After an incident in 1941 when a spitball was mischievously thrown at Calloway (he accused Gillespie but the culprit was actually Jonah Jones), Dizzy was fired.
By then, Gillespie had already met Charlie Parker, who confirmed the validity of his musical search. During 1941-1943, Dizzy passed through many bands including those led by Ella Fitzgerald, Coleman Hawkins, Benny Carter, Charlie Barnet, Fess Williams, Les Hite, Claude Hopkins, Lucky Millinder (with whom he recorded in 1942), and even Duke Ellington (for four weeks). Gillespie also contributed several advanced arrangements to such bands as Benny Carter, Jimmy Dorsey, and Woody Herman; the latter advised him to give up his trumpet playing and stick to full-time arranging.
texts.2:
Dizzy ignored the advice, jammed at Minton’s Playhouse and Monroe’s Uptown House where he tried out his new ideas, and in late 1942 joined Earl Hines’ big band. Charlie Parker was hired on tenor and the sadly unrecorded orchestra was the first orchestra to explore early bebop. By then, Gillespie had his style together and he wrote his most famous composition “A Night in Tunisia.” When Hines’ singer Billy Eckstine went on his own and formed a new bop big band, Diz and Bird (along with Sarah Vaughan) were among the members. Gillespie stayed long enough to record a few numbers with Eckstine in 1944 (most noticeably “Opus X” and “Blowing the Blues Away”). That year he also participated in a pair of Coleman Hawkins-led sessions that are often thought of as the first full-fledged bebop dates, highlighted by Dizzy’s composition “Woody’n You.”
1945 was the breakthrough year. Dizzy Gillespie, who had led earlier bands on 52nd Street, finally teamed up with Charlie Parker on records. Their recordings of such numbers as “Salt Peanuts,” “‘Shaw Nuff,” “Groovin’ High,” and “Hot House” confused swing fans who had never heard the advanced music as it was evolving; and Dizzy’s rendition of “I Can’t Get Started” completely reworked the former Bunny Berigan hit. It would take two years for the often frantic but ultimately logical new style to start catching on as the mainstream of jazz. Gillespie led an unsuccessful big band in 1945 (a Southern tour finished it), and late in the year he traveled with Parker to the West Coast to play a lengthy gig at Billy Berg’s club in L.A. Unfortunately, the audiences were not enthusiastic (other than local musicians) and Dizzy (without Parker) soon returned to New York.
texts.3: The following year, Dizzy Gillespie put together a successful and influential orchestra which survived for nearly four memorable years. “Manteca” became a standard, the exciting “Things to Come” was futuristic, and “Cubana Be/Cubana Bop” featured Chano Pozo. With such sidemen as the future original members of the Modern Jazz Quartet (Milt Jackson, John Lewis, Ray Brown, and Kenny Clarke), James Moody, J.J. Johnson, Yusef Lateef, and even a young John Coltrane, Gillespie’s big band was a breeding ground for the new music. Dizzy’s beret, goatee, and “bop glasses” helped make him a symbol of the music and its most popular figure. During 1948-1949, nearly every former swing band was trying to play bop, and for a brief period the major record companies tried very hard to turn the music into a fad.
texts.4:
By 1950, the fad had ended and Gillespie was forced, due to economic pressures, to break up his groundbreaking orchestra. He had occasional (and always exciting) reunions with Charlie Parker (including a fabled Massey Hall concert in 1953) up until Bird’s death in 1955, toured with Jazz at the Philharmonic (where he had opportunities to “battle” the combative Roy Eldridge), headed all-star recording sessions (using Stan Getz, Sonny Rollins, and Sonny Stitt on some dates), and led combos that for a time in 1951 also featured Coltrane and Milt Jackson. In 1956, Gillespie was authorized to form a big band and play a tour overseas sponsored by the State Department. It was so successful that more traveling followed, including extensive tours to the Near East, Europe, and South America, and the band survived up to 1958. Among the young sidemen were Lee Morgan, Joe Gordon, Melba Liston, Al Grey, Billy Mitchell, Benny Golson, Ernie Henry, and Wynton Kelly; Quincy Jones (along with Golson and Liston) contributed some of the arrangements. After the orchestra broke up, Gillespie went back to leading small groups, featuring such sidemen in the 1960s as Junior Mance, Leo Wright, Lalo Schifrin, James Moody, and Kenny Barron. He retained his popularity, occasionally headed specially assembled big bands, and was a fixture at jazz festivals. In the early ’70s, Gillespie toured with the Giants of Jazz and around that time his trumpet playing began to fade, a gradual decline that would make most of his ’80s work quite erratic. However, Dizzy remained a world traveler, an inspiration and teacher to younger players, and during his last couple of years he was the leader of the United Nation Orchestra (featuring Paquito D’Rivera and Arturo Sandoval). He was active up until early 1992.
Dizzy Gillespie’s career was very well documented from 1945 on, particularly on Musicraft, Dial, and RCA in the 1940s; Verve in the 1950s; Philips and Limelight in the 1960s; and Pablo in later years. ~ Scott Yanow

*   Context: Coltrane (tenor/sometimes alto) sat in with Gillespie’s groups and toured intermittently as a young player in the post‑war bebop scene. Documentation is fragmentary but corroborated by memoirs, union logs and sessionographies.  
*   Typical repertoire: bebop standards commonly played by Gillespie’s band at the time — “Groovin’ High,” “A Night in Tunisia,” “Salt Peanuts,” “Hot House.” These tunes were staples of Gillespie’s setlist and Coltrane would have been exposed to and likely performed them during these engagements.
2) Live club appearances and jam sessions (1947–1949)
*   Notable reports: Coltrane played in New York clubs where Gillespie led or dropped by (e.g., Royal Roost, Minton’s). Specific contemporaneous setlists were rarely documented, but eyewitness accounts and later interviews place Coltrane on bills where Gillespie’s groups played bebop repertoire.  
*   Typical tunes: extended bebop jam vehicles and standards — “Con Alma,” “I Can’t Get Started,” “All the Things You Are,” and the Gillespie hits listed above.
3) 1950s reunion/encounters
*   Context: Occasional later encounters between the two occurred on festivals and all‑star concerts. These were one‑off performances rather than formal tours.  
*   Example repertoire: When appearing together at festivals the songs were usually Gillespie’s or jazz standards arranged for short sets; specific reliable track lists are sparse.
Recordings and authoritative sources

*   No major studio recording exists with Coltrane as a clearly credited soloist under Gillespie’s name from the 1940s. Most evidence of their playing together comes from live gig listings, musician recollections, union records and secondary discographies.  
*   Useful references: Lewis Porter’s Coltrane discography and biography, Ashley Kahn’s Coltrane biographies, Dizzy Gillespie discographies and contemporary jazz periodicals (DownBeat archives). These sources summarize appearances and corroborate the pattern: Coltrane worked with Gillespie early in his career but left no widely circulated studio tracks as a featured sideman for Dizzy.
Practical summary
*   Yes — Coltrane did play with Dizzy Gillespie, mainly in the late 1940s during live gigs and short engagements.  
*   Specific songs they likely played together are Gillespie’s bebop staples: “Groovin’ High,” “A Night in Tunisia,” “Salt Peanuts,” and standard jazz repertoire common in jam sessions.  
*   No well‑known commercial studio recordings exist that feature Coltrane as a credited soloist with Gillespie; evidence is strongest in live/bootleg contexts and through biographical documentation.
John Coltrane did indeed play with Dizzy Gillespie…and played with Diz’s bebop big band in 1949. There is a famous photo from Birdland, with Charlie Parker & Dizzy from 1950…which shows a young Coltrane in the background. This photo is sometimes cropped, and Trane is not shown in it. Coltrane recorded with Gillespie on some small group sessions from 1951. They were released on a small label…and can be found, if one wants to do the searching. Trane’s style in ’51 was more R&B flavored,due to Gillespie’s band orientation in those days. Bebop as a trend…was fading..and Diz had to make a living. That’s why the band’s repetoire consisted of novelty tunes,standards and of course, the blues.

Did John Coltrane ever meet Miles Davis?
Yes, John Coltrane did meet Miles Davis. They both played together in the group of the legendary jazz trumpeter and bandleader, Miles Davis. Coltrane joined Davis' band in 1955 and stayed with the group until 1957. During that period, they recorded several albums together, including "Round About Midnight" and "Relaxin' With The Miles Davis Quintet" . Coltrane's time with Davis' band was a formative period in his career, and he credited Davis with helping him to develop his own style. Dizzy Gillespie’s contributions to jazz were huge. One of the greatest jazz trumpeters of all time (some would say the best), Gillespie was such a complex player that his contemporaries ended up copying Miles Davis and Fats Navarro instead, and it was not until Jon Faddis’ emergence in the 1970s that Dizzy’s style was successfully recreated. Somehow, Gillespie could make any “wrong” note fit, and harmonically he was ahead of everyone in the 1940s, including Charlie Parker. Unlike Bird, Dizzy was an enthusiastic teacher who wrote down his musical innovations and was eager to explain them to the next generation, thereby insuring that bebop would eventually become the foundation of jazz.
Dizzy Gillespie was also one of the key founders of Afro-Cuban (or Latin) jazz, adding Chano Pozo’s conga to his orchestra in 1947, and utilizing complex poly-rhythms early on. The leader of two of the finest big bands in jazz history, Gillespie differed from many in the bop generation by being a masterful showman who could make his music seem both accessible and fun to the audience. With his puffed-out cheeks, bent trumpet (which occurred by accident in the early ’50s when a dancer tripped over his horn), and quick wit, Dizzy was a colorful figure to watch. A natural comedian, Gillespie was also a superb scat singer and occasionally played Latin percussion for the fun of it, but it was his trumpet playing and leadership abilities that made him into a jazz giant.

The youngest of nine children, John Birks Gillespie taught himself trombone and then switched to trumpet when he was 12. He grew up in poverty, won a scholarship to an agricultural school (Laurinburg Institute in North Carolina), and then in 1935 dropped out of school to look for work as a musician. Inspired and initially greatly influenced by Roy Eldridge, Gillespie (who soon gained the nickname of “Dizzy”) joined Frankie Fairfax’s band in Philadelphia. In 1937, he became a member of Teddy Hill’s orchestra in a spot formerly filled by Eldridge. Dizzy made his recording debut on Hill’s rendition of “King Porter Stomp” and during his short period with the band toured Europe. After freelancing for a year, Gillespie joined Cab Calloway’s orchestra (1939-1941), recording frequently with the popular bandleader and taking many short solos that trace his development; “Pickin’ the Cabbage” finds Dizzy starting to emerge from Eldridge’s shadow. However, Calloway did not care for Gillespie’s constant chance-taking, calling his solos “Chinese music.” After an incident in 1941 when a spitball was mischievously thrown at Calloway (he accused Gillespie but the culprit was actually Jonah Jones), Dizzy was fired.
By then, Gillespie had already met Charlie Parker, who confirmed the validity of his musical search. During 1941-1943, Dizzy passed through many bands including those led by Ella Fitzgerald, Coleman Hawkins, Benny Carter, Charlie Barnet, Fess Williams, Les Hite, Claude Hopkins, Lucky Millinder (with whom he recorded in 1942), and even Duke Ellington (for four weeks). Gillespie also contributed several advanced arrangements to such bands as Benny Carter, Jimmy Dorsey, and Woody Herman; the latter advised him to give up his trumpet playing and stick to full-time arranging.

Dizzy ignored the advice, jammed at Minton’s Playhouse and Monroe’s Uptown House where he tried out his new ideas, and in late 1942 joined Earl Hines’ big band. Charlie Parker was hired on tenor and the sadly unrecorded orchestra was the first orchestra to explore early bebop. By then, Gillespie had his style together and he wrote his most famous composition “A Night in Tunisia.” When Hines’ singer Billy Eckstine went on his own and formed a new bop big band, Diz and Bird (along with Sarah Vaughan) were among the members. Gillespie stayed long enough to record a few numbers with Eckstine in 1944 (most noticeably “Opus X” and “Blowing the Blues Away”). That year he also participated in a pair of Coleman Hawkins-led sessions that are often thought of as the first full-fledged bebop dates, highlighted by Dizzy’s composition “Woody’n You.”
1945 was the breakthrough year. Dizzy Gillespie, who had led earlier bands on 52nd Street, finally teamed up with Charlie Parker on records. Their recordings of such numbers as “Salt Peanuts,” “‘Shaw Nuff,” “Groovin’ High,” and “Hot House” confused swing fans who had never heard the advanced music as it was evolving; and Dizzy’s rendition of “I Can’t Get Started” completely reworked the former Bunny Berigan hit. It would take two years for the often frantic but ultimately logical new style to start catching on as the mainstream of jazz. Gillespie led an unsuccessful big band in 1945 (a Southern tour finished it), and late in the year he traveled with Parker to the West Coast to play a lengthy gig at Billy Berg’s club in L.A. Unfortunately, the audiences were not enthusiastic (other than local musicians) and Dizzy (without Parker) soon returned to New York.

The following year, Dizzy Gillespie put together a successful and influential orchestra which survived for nearly four memorable years. “Manteca” became a standard, the exciting “Things to Come” was futuristic, and “Cubana Be/Cubana Bop” featured Chano Pozo. With such sidemen as the future original members of the Modern Jazz Quartet (Milt Jackson, John Lewis, Ray Brown, and Kenny Clarke), James Moody, J.J. Johnson, Yusef Lateef, and even a young John Coltrane, Gillespie’s big band was a breeding ground for the new music. Dizzy’s beret, goatee, and “bop glasses” helped make him a symbol of the music and its most popular figure. During 1948-1949, nearly every former swing band was trying to play bop, and for a brief period the major record companies tried very hard to turn the music into a fad.

By 1950, the fad had ended and Gillespie was forced, due to economic pressures, to break up his groundbreaking orchestra. He had occasional (and always exciting) reunions with Charlie Parker (including a fabled Massey Hall concert in 1953) up until Bird’s death in 1955, toured with Jazz at the Philharmonic (where he had opportunities to “battle” the combative Roy Eldridge), headed all-star recording sessions (using Stan Getz, Sonny Rollins, and Sonny Stitt on some dates), and led combos that for a time in 1951 also featured Coltrane and Milt Jackson. In 1956, Gillespie was authorized to form a big band and play a tour overseas sponsored by the State Department. It was so successful that more traveling followed, including extensive tours to the Near East, Europe, and South America, and the band survived up to 1958. Among the young sidemen were Lee Morgan, Joe Gordon, Melba Liston, Al Grey, Billy Mitchell, Benny Golson, Ernie Henry, and Wynton Kelly; Quincy Jones (along with Golson and Liston) contributed some of the arrangements. After the orchestra broke up, Gillespie went back to leading small groups, featuring such sidemen in the 1960s as Junior Mance, Leo Wright, Lalo Schifrin, James Moody, and Kenny Barron. He retained his popularity, occasionally headed specially assembled big bands, and was a fixture at jazz festivals. In the early ’70s, Gillespie toured with the Giants of Jazz and around that time his trumpet playing began to fade, a gradual decline that would make most of his ’80s work quite erratic. However, Dizzy remained a world traveler, an inspiration and teacher to younger players, and during his last couple of years he was the leader of the United Nation Orchestra (featuring Paquito D’Rivera and Arturo Sandoval). He was active up until early 1992.
Dizzy Gillespie’s career was very well documented from 1945 on, particularly on Musicraft, Dial, and RCA in the 1940s; Verve in the 1950s; Philips and Limelight in the 1960s; and Pablo in later years. ~ Scott Yanow

**Shellac releases featuring Dizzy Gillespie and John Coltrane – tracks where Gillespie is credited as writer** | Shellac release (10″/78 RPM) | Track(s) credited to Gillespie | Evidence | |------------------------------|--------------------------------|----------| | *Dizzy Gillespie And His Orchestra – “Tally‑Ho” / “I Can’t Remember”* (Capitol 839, U.S., 1950) | **Tally‑Ho** | Tracklist shows “Written‑By – Dizzy Gillespie”【6†L51-L58】; Coltrane appears in the credits list (un‑credited Alto‑Sax)【6†L59-L65】 | | *Dizzy Gillespie And His Orchestra – “Coast To Coast” / “Oo‑la‑la”* (Telefunken Capitol 450, France, 1951) | **Coast To Coast** (Written‑By – Buster Hardeng, D. Gillespie)
**Oo‑la‑la** (Written‑By – Gillespie, Williams, Acea) | Both tracks list “Written‑By – Dizzy Gillespie” in the track‑listing【6†L27-L35】; Coltrane is credited for saxophone on the release【6†L37-L43】 | | *Dizzy Gillespie – “Tin Tin Daeo” / “Birks Works”* (Dee Gee 3600, U.S., 1951) | **Birks Works** | Tracklist shows “Written‑By – Dizzy Gillespie”【6†L33-L40】; Coltrane is credited as tenor‑saxophone on the release【6†L41-L48】 | --- ### Why these tracks qualify 1. **Shellac format** – All four releases are 78 rpm/10″ shellac discs (Discogs lists “Shellac, 10”, 78 RPM”). 2. **John Coltrane in personnel** – Each release lists Coltrane in the “Credits” section (either as “Alto Saxophone” or “Tenor Saxophone”, often un‑credited in the track‑listing but present overall). 3. **Gillespie credited as writer** – The track‑listing clearly shows a “Written‑By” credit that includes Dizzy Gillespie (either alone or co‑writer). These are the only tracks on the qualifying shellac releases that meet that criterion. **Summary** The shellac records of Dizzy Gillespie that feature John Coltrane and contain tracks where Gillespie is the writer are: - **Tally‑Ho** – *Tally‑Ho / I Can’t Remember* (Capitol 839, 1950) - **Coast To Coast** – *Coast To Coast / Oo‑la‑la* (Telefunken Capitol 450, 1951) - **Oo‑la‑la** – *Coast To Coast / Oo‑la‑la* (same record) - **Birks Works** – *Tin Tin Daeo / Birks Works* (Dee Gee 3600, 1951) These are the only shellac tracks that satisfy both “contains Coltrane” and “written‑by Gillespie” conditions.
